story_text.value:
Like instagram, but all photos have a shelf life: they can be up for year, an hour or ten minutes, or up until they're viewed 100 times, 1000 times or a million times, etc.

The longer they're up, the more they fade - user chosen filters are applied gradually over the lifetime of the photo (be it measured in clicks or time), gradually obscuring it. At the end of its lifetime, the pictures faded / expired, and disappears, though comments remain.

This is a fun side project of mine, An experiment in digital persistence and scarcity. And, yes its vibe coded, built on replit.

Currently just a responsive web page (desktop, and works great on iOS devices, which I have). Native apps for android and iOS to follow should interest and time permit!

title.value: Show HN: Digital scarcity; app where photos gradually decay with time / views

story_text.value:
I built Soulor independently as a 16y/o high school student. It helps reading social situations with multiple perspectives, and helps users rehearse hard conversations by simulating others with analyses and suggestions, there are also companions that knows the full context if users choose to share that can chat with them naturally. It can be both serious and entertaining, by switching different world views, and it fully respects users' privacy by keeping all texts encrypted.

In order to achieve modest performance, I built multi-regional gateway and a fine-tuned model integrating both quality and responding speed. The models are served on GPUs via Modal, with a second adapter just for the simulation, and reply latency went from 7.9s to about 2.0s.

It already has several users and I'm building it up quickly. Happy to answer questions about the app or the tech, and any feedback is welcome.

Pretty self-explanatory tbh. I kept hitting the same friction using LeetCode, the built-in editor has no real language support and none of the Vim muscle memory I rely on everywhere else. So I started building it in.

This is also where I love AI, I had started to work on it years ago, at first it was only snippets of most used classes (vector, string, etc...) and a few vim keymaps. Being able to tell Codex "Improve this, make no mistakes" is pretty fun.

Also side note, I've always used Leetcode as a game to practice problem solving (Graph Algorithms <3333), but I feel like now more than ever it is a good platform to code manually and challenge yourself, especially when vibe coding is so present. (I don't recommend grinding if you don't enjoy it tho)

story_text.value:
Basically, I didn't want to waste my opus 5.5 or codex Astra credits just to find files in my machine, so I trained a local LLM which is only 1.5B to write bash to find files on your macos laptop (works on apple silicon, uses little ram).

Full privacy since it's local so you can look for your sensitive files and api keys without sending them to a third party server.

It outperforms strong cloud models like Gemini 3.8 Flash and hefty 31B Param Gemma models in the file search benchmark I created to measure competency, details here: https://shlexball.com/findbench/

title.value: Show HN: Shlexball, describe a file and a local 1.5B model finds it on your Mac

story_text.value: A kernel guard I prototyped after eBPF and vTPM work for a customer, where we use the TPM to protect the private keys for mTLS. Any process running as root can open the TPM devices, and so can any process in the `tss` group, through `/dev/tpmrm0`. That means they can use those keys too. This is a prototype and some research into protecting this path.

story_text.value:
MapLibre Compose is a Kotlin library for putting interactive vector maps in Compose Multiplatform apps on Android, iOS, desktop, and web. It's part of the MapLibre ecosystem, and isn't tied to any map provider; you point it at any MapLibre style and tile source: commercial, free, or your own.

- Docs: https://maplibre.org/maplibre-compose/

- Code: https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-compose

- Live demo: https://maplibre.org/maplibre-compose/demo/

About two years ago, I started building a transit tracking app in Compose Multiplatform, and found there was no suitable map library for it with the level of customization I wanted. So, within my "train-tracking-app" repo, I started working on wrapping the MapLibre Android and iOS SDKs behind a common Compose API.

Around the same time, the StreetComplete folks and MapLibre Native folks were looking for the same thing: a Compose SDK for MapLibre Native. I spun my wrapper out into a library, and so began my two year yak shaving quest to bring MapLibre maps to Compose Multiplatform.

The SDK-wrapping approach got the first releases out quickly, but it didn't age well. I could only expose what both supported, and each had its own slightly different design and API contracts, as they were not designed to be used together. And there was no such sdk at all for desktop. I knew I needed to go a layer down, build on the MapLibre Native C++ core underpinning those Android and iOS SDKs. I first did this with JNI, on desktop only, with the help of GLM-4.5 to navigate some graphics work that I was deeply unfamiliar with. This worked, but JNI was tedious and bug-prone, AWT<>Compose interop was limited, and the work stalled. Around this time, I also onboarded the project into the MapLibre organization.

Earlier this year, I rebooted the native core wrapping effort. I designed a C API (https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-native-ffi) wrapping the MapLibre Native C++ core, generated safe(ish) language bindings on top for KMP and many other languages (first with LLMs, now working on deterministic codegen), and rebuilt MapLibre Compose for desktop, Android, and iOS on that foundation. This cleared numerous blockers and bugs, and allowed me to bring the library to a feature-complete state.

This work shipped in the StreetComplete iOS public beta recently (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49920160). Stadia's Ferrostar navigation SDK builds on it now too (https://stadiamaps.github.io/ferrostar/).

It's pre-1.0. Android, iOS, and desktop wrap MapLibre Native. Kotlin/JS still wraps MapLibre GL JS, and Kotlin/Wasm support is awaiting Compose v1.13. If you're interested in building map apps with Compose, I encourage you to try this out and share feedback as I'm working on refining the api surface before stabilization.

Now, two years later, I'm getting back to working on my transit tracking app, which I hope to share on HN in a couple months.

story_text.value:
I was frustrated with Google Analytics and Plausible, and I wanted something simple that highlighted actionable things I could focus on to improve revenue. Less focus on vanity metrics like pageviews, instead just showing where revenue comes from. That tells you what's the most profitable and best use of your time, at a glance. So I built the tool I wanted.

One of the first side projects I ever worked on was a web analytics tool back when I was teaching myself how to code almost 25 years ago when I was 18.

So it feels like coming full circle to actually build a web analytics tool.

I've always struggled to finish side projects and do the last 20% of polish (which takes 80% of the time somehow). Coding and building things is fun, but that work is tedious. I credit AI with making it easier to the point where I can actually finish side projects now.

I'm very interested in what others think and how I could improve it. Be honest, but gentle please :)
